\begin{schema}{SendState}
  smtpAvailable : ZBOOL \\
  signingRequired : ZBOOL \\
  method! : SendMethod
  \where
  (smtpAvailable = ztrue \implies method! = smSMTP) \\
  \land \\
  (smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signingRequired = zfalse
    \implies method! = smResend) \\
  \land \\
  (smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signingRequired = ztrue
    \implies method! = smFailed)
\end{schema}

The send path attempts the configured SMTP transport first.  If that
transport is unreachable (a TCP dial to the SMTP port times out in
2~seconds), the Resend API is used as fallback --- unless the
outbound message must be PGP-signed or encrypted, in which case
there is no fallback at all: Resend has no raw-MIME API and cannot
preserve a \texttt{multipart/signed} or \texttt{multipart/encrypted}
envelope, so the send fails outright ($method! = smFailed$).
\textit{SendState} models which \emph{route} is chosen, not whether
the chosen route actually preserved the envelope it composed ---
\texttt{TrySendChain} does not itself verify that the SMTP host it
dials preserves \texttt{multipart/signed}, so $method! = smSMTP
\land signingRequired = ztrue$ can report success on a host that
silently strips the signature.  That is a filed defect, not a
property this schema asserts or checks.

tool_input.new_string:
\subsection{PGP Signing (Future)}

PGP signing of outbound mail requires a transport that preserves raw
MIME (\texttt{multipart/signed} envelopes).  Neither Proton Bridge
(strips MIME) nor Resend (no raw MIME API) supports this.  Amazon
SES will be added as the PGP-signing transport in a future release.
tool_input.old_string:
\subsection{PGP Signing and Encryption}

Outbound PGP signing is implemented, not future work: when
\texttt{cfg.GPGSigner} is configured, every message sent over Proton
Bridge SMTP is signed (RFC~3156 \texttt{multipart/signed}); when
recipient key IDs are also supplied, the message is signed then
encrypted (RFC~3156 \texttt{multipart/encrypted}).  Proton Bridge
preserves the raw MIME envelope when reached directly over SMTP ---
the transport limitation this section previously described applied
to routing through Bridge's own UI/webmail path, not to
\texttt{beadle-email}'s direct SMTP connection.  Resend remains
signing-incapable (no raw MIME API), which is why $signingRequired =
ztrue$ removes it as a fallback rather than silently sending an
unsigned copy.

tool_input.new_string:
\begin{zed}
  SendMethod ::= smSMTP | smResend | smFailed
\end{zed}

Outbound messages use the configured SMTP transport as the primary
route (Proton Bridge in the default configuration; a MIME-preserving
host such as Fastmail when PGP signing is configured, since Bridge
strips \texttt{multipart/signed}), falling back to Resend API when
that transport is unavailable, or failing outright when signing is
required and no fallback can carry it.

The classification is total: every combination of inputs maps to
exactly one trust level.  Proton E2E takes priority over PGP
signatures (a Proton-internal message with a PGP signature is
still $trusted$, not $verified$).

\subsection{External Origin: An Assumption, Not a Theorem}

\texttt{ClassifyTrust} proves that every combination of its four
$ZBOOL$ inputs is mapped to exactly one $TrustLevel$ (a routine case
split on $hasProtonE2E$, $hasProtonInternal$, $hasPGPSignature$, and
$pgpVerified$, each of which has only two values).  It does \emph{not}
prove the stronger property this repository actually depends on: that
no externally-originated message is ever classified $trusted$.  It
cannot, because nothing in $TrustInput$ says where a message came
from --- $hasProtonE2E$ and $hasProtonInternal$ are bare booleans, and
the schema has no way to ask whether they are telling the truth.

\begin{zed}
  Origin ::= originInternal | originExternal
\end{zed}

\begin{schema}{ChannelAssumption}
  origin : Origin \\
  hasProtonE2E : ZBOOL \\
  hasProtonInternal : ZBOOL
  \where
  origin = originExternal \implies
    \lnot (hasProtonE2E = ztrue \land hasProtonInternal = ztrue)
\end{schema}

$origin$ is ground truth: where the message actually came from, not
what its headers claim.  \texttt{ChannelAssumption} is not derived
from anything else in this document --- it is posited, and its truth
depends entirely on Proton Bridge behaving as documented (setting
\texttt{X-Pm-Content-Encryption}/\texttt{X-Pm-Origin} only for
messages it has itself routed end-to-end between two Proton
mailboxes, and stripping or refusing to forward those headers on
anything externally injected).  \texttt{internal/daemon/handler.go}
records the same assumption in a code comment rather than an
enforced check: \textit{``External SMTP injection of these headers is
blocked by Bridge''} --- exactly the kind of claim a Z schema cannot
verify and should not pretend to.

Given \texttt{ChannelAssumption}, the property this repository relies
on follows as a theorem, not as decoration: by \texttt{ClassifyTrust},
$hasProtonE2E = ztrue \land hasProtonInternal = ztrue$ is the only
condition that entails $level! = trusted$, and by the totality proved
above no other input combination also entails it; by
\texttt{ChannelAssumption}'s contrapositive, that same condition
entails $origin = originInternal$.  So $level! = trusted \implies
origin = originInternal$ --- \emph{no external sender is ever
trusted} --- but only for as long as \texttt{ChannelAssumption} holds.
If Bridge is ever misconfigured, or a future defect lets an external
SMTP client set these two headers, this specification gives no
warning: the assumption, not a theorem about message content, is
where that guarantee actually lives.

\subsection{Two-Phase Trust Resolution}

tool_input.new_string:
\begin{schema}{SendState}
  smtpAvailable : ZBOOL \\
  signingRequired : ZBOOL \\
  method! : SendMethod
  \where
  (smtpAvailable = ztrue \implies method! = smSMTP) \\
  \land \\
  (smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signingRequired = zfalse
    \implies method! = smResend) \\
  \land \\
  (smtpAvailable = zfalse \land signingRequired = ztrue
    \implies method! = smFailed)
\end{schema}

The send path attempts the configured SMTP transport first.  If that
transport is unreachable (a TCP dial to the SMTP port times out in
2~seconds), the Resend API is used as fallback --- unless the
outbound message must be PGP-signed or encrypted, in which case
there is no fallback at all: Resend has no raw-MIME API and cannot
preserve a \texttt{multipart/signed} or \texttt{multipart/encrypted}
envelope, so the send fails outright ($method! = smFailed$).
\texttt{SendState} models which \emph{route} is chosen, not whether
the chosen route actually preserved the envelope it composed --- see
\S~PGP Signing for the transport-validation gap that leaves.

tool_input.new_string:
\begin{schema}{VerifyEnvironment}
  systemKeys : \power KEYID \\
  importedKeys : \power KEYID \\
  isolated : ZBOOL
  \where
  isolated = ztrue \\
  importedKeys \subseteq systemKeys
\end{schema}

\texttt{VerifyEnvironment} models \emph{inbound signature
verification only}.  The $isolated = ztrue$ invariant does not hold
for the PGP subsystem as a whole: the Sign Flow below, and
decryption, deliberately use the caller's own system keyring
(\texttt{internal/pgp/sign.go}, \texttt{decrypt.go}) because that is
where the owner's private key already lives, and no isolated homedir
could sign or decrypt with it.  Do not read this schema, or Key
Property~3 below, as a claim about signing or decryption --- both
are the one part of the PGP subsystem that is intentionally not
isolated, by the same Design Invariant~3 that states it in prose.

Every verification runs in an isolated GNUPGHOME under
\texttt{/tmp/bg-*}.  The short path prefix avoids the 108-byte
Unix socket path limit for \texttt{gpg-agent}.
